items.name: Gem and jewellery resale scam
items.what_happens: Merchants sell lower-quality gems or jewellery at inflated prices, promising the items can be resold at a profit; the guarantees they offer are not always honoured.
items.avoid: Do not buy gems or jewellery as an investment or on a resale promise, and think carefully before any purchase if you are not knowledgeable about gems.

sources.quote: merchants sell lower-quality items at inflated prices with promises that the items can be resold at a profit

items.name: Bar or nightclub overcharging
items.what_happens: Some bars, nightclubs and entertainment venues try to charge exorbitant prices, and arguments over the bill can lead to threats of violence.
items.avoid: Confirm prices before you order, avoid running a tab, and do not leave your credit card with bar or restaurant staff.

sources.quote: Some bars, nightclubs and entertainment venues may try to charge exorbitant prices. Discussions about overcharging may lead to threats of violence.

items.name: Rental damage claim / passport held as deposit
items.what_happens: Motorbike or jet-ski rental businesses may claim you damaged the vehicle and keep the passport you left as a guarantee; renters who refused to pay have been harassed and threatened.
items.avoid: Never hand over your passport as collateral, read the rental contract, photograph existing damage before you ride, and rent only from reputable companies.

sources.quote: Do not hand your passport over as a guarantee, for example to motorcycle or jet-ski rental businesses.
Rental companies have at times accused renters of causing damage upon return of the equipment.

items.name: Drink spiking
items.what_happens: Drinks have been spiked in tourist areas, with drug-assisted sexual assault and robbery affecting both men and women.
items.avoid: Do not leave drinks unattended or accept drinks, snacks or cigarettes from strangers, and pre-arrange your transport home.

sources.quote: Drink spiking and drug-assisted sexual assault does happen in tourist areas around Thailand, with male and female victims.
Never leave food or drinks unattended or in the care of strangers.

items.name: Card skimming and ATM fraud
items.what_happens: Card fraud happens, including ATM skimming and cards being misused while out of your sight during transactions.
items.avoid: Keep your card in sight, use ATMs inside banks, cover the keypad when entering your PIN, and check your statements.

sources.quote: Do not lose sight of your card during transactions. There have been incidents of ATM skimming. Use an ATM in a bank
pay careful attention when your cards are being handled by others

items.name: Unlicensed taxis and tuk-tuk disputes
items.what_happens: Unlicensed vehicles may not use meters and are not correctly insured to carry passengers, and fare disputes with taxi or tuk-tuk operators have occasionally turned violent or intimidating.
items.avoid: Use licensed taxis from official stands, a trusted ride-hailing app, or the airport rail link; if a dispute turns threatening, ask local police for help.

sources.quote: Disputes with taxis operators, tuk-tuks (motorized rickshaws), etc., occur and have occasionally resulted in violence or intimidation.
Unlicensed vehicles (bearing black and white licence plates) are not correctly insured to carry passengers and may not use meters.

items.name: Distraction pickpocketing
items.what_happens: Thieves use distraction techniques, such as spilling a drink on you, engaging you in long conversations or persistently offering help, to take your belongings, especially in city centres, at tourist sites and on public transport.
items.avoid: Keep your belongings in sight, be wary of unsolicited offers or help from strangers, and do not carry all your valuables together.

sources.quote: beware of thieves using distraction techniques
spill drinks on you or your belongings

items.avoid: Use only licensed taxis from an official rank, by phone or by app, or the authorised vehicles in the airport's designated areas.

items.name: Fake car fault / help-me stop
items.what_happens: Thieves may get you to stop your car by asking for help or directions or by pointing out a fake fault, then steal from it; thefts from parked cars and snatches at traffic lights are common.
items.avoid: Do not stop for strangers flagging a problem, keep doors locked and windows closed, and never leave luggage in the car, even in the boot.

sources.quote: pointing out a fictional fault with your car
never leave belongings unattended in a vehicle, even in the trunk

sources.publisher: Préfecture de police de Paris (via French Ministry of the Interior)
sources.quote: le maître du jeu est assisté de complices qui se font passer pour des joueurs

items.avoid: Use only official taxi ranks at airports and never accept a ride from someone offering transport in the terminal, station or street.

sources.publisher: Préfecture de police de Paris (via French Ministry of the Interior)
sources.quote: Certains escrocs peuvent se faire passer pour des policiers et vous demander vos papiers et de l’argent.

items.name: Street ticket resellers and touting cabarets
items.what_happens: Unofficial ticket resellers at stations can charge far more than the real price, and some cabarets tout on the street and then make customers buy very expensive drinks.
items.avoid: Buy tickets only at station counters and machines or from official resellers, and avoid venues that pull customers in off the pavement.

items.name: Fake plain-clothes police

items.avoid: Genuine police ask for ID but never for your wallet or purse; ask to see their official identification badge.

items.name: Something's wrong with your car
items.what_happens: Thieves flag you down claiming there is a problem with your car (such as a flat tyre) or that you damaged theirs, then steal the car or your belongings when you stop.
items.avoid: Do not trust anyone who tells you something is wrong with your car; stop only somewhere public and lit, such as a petrol station.

items.name: Street money changers

items.name: The "mustard" spill distraction
items.what_happens: Someone sprays mustard or another substance on you, and while an accomplice "helps" clean it off, your bags are taken. Thieves, often women, work in teams.
items.avoid: Politely but firmly refuse help and walk away, keeping hold of your bags.

sources.quote: A common form of distraction theft reported in Buenos Aires is the 'mustard scam'.
spraying a substance on victims and then robbing them while pretending to help clean the stain

items.name: Phone lifted under merchandise at café tables
items.what_happens: A street seller puts merchandise such as dishcloths or socks on top of your phone at a restaurant table, then picks up the phone along with it.
items.avoid: Keep your phone off the table, especially on terraces, and be suspicious of vendors who approach your table.

sources.quote: putting merchandise such as dishcloths or socks on top of your phone at restaurants and picking up your phone along with the merchandise

items.name: Fake "hotel guests" at check-in
items.what_happens: Thieves posing as hotel guests snatch bags while you are checking in.
items.avoid: Keep your bags close, or between your feet, at hotel and hostel reception.

sources.quote: keep your bags close while you are checking into a hotel or hostel - thieves posing as hotel guests can snatch them

items.name: Counterfeit change from taxis and unofficial airport taxis
items.what_happens: Unscrupulous taxi drivers sometimes swap your good banknotes for counterfeit ones; at Ezeiza (Ministro Pistarini) airport only officially marked taxis should be used.
items.avoid: Pay with exact change, book a taxi by app or use a radio taxi with a visible door logo, and use the official taxi stand in the airport arrivals area.

sources.quote: Try to pay with exact change, since unscrupulous taxi drivers sometimes trade counterfeit bills for good ones
If you hail a taxi in the street, only use a 'radio taxi'. These have a clearly visible logo on the car doors.
Only use officially marked taxis for travel to and from Buenos Aires' Ministro Pistarini International Airport.

items.name: Followed from ATMs and exchange bureaus
items.what_happens: Criminals wait outside ATMs and casas de cambio, or follow people after they withdraw or exchange money.
items.avoid: Use indoor ATMs in hotels or supermarkets, avoid ATMs at night, and use official exchange bureaus only.

sources.quote: or follow a victim after they exchange or withdraw money
Use official exchange bureaus

items.name: Express kidnapping
items.what_happens: Victims are briefly abducted and forced to empty their bank accounts by transfer or at ATMs; FCDO links the risk to casual taxis.
items.avoid: Avoid casual street taxis, do not flaunt expensive items, and let someone know where you are.

sources.quote: Victims of express kidnap are held and forced to empty their bank accounts by making bank transfers or going to ATMs
express kidnappings involving tourists have occurred in Argentina

items.name: Spiking and robbery by new acquaintances
items.what_happens: Food and drinks can be spiked, and tourists have been robbed or assaulted after inviting someone they had just met, online or in person, back to their accommodation.
items.avoid: Do not leave drinks unattended, do not accept food or drink from strangers, and be cautious about inviting new acquaintances to where you are staying.

sources.quote: There have been reports of foreign tourists being robbed or assaulted after inviting into their accommodation someone they have recently met, online or in person.
Drinks and food can be spiked and could put you at risk of robbery or assault.

buenos-aires-argentina.notes: FCDO names Buenos Aires for the mustard scam and lists BA hotspots (Palermo, San Telmo, La Boca, Florida Street, Retiro and others); Canada names BA tourist areas and Ezeiza airport. The phone/merchandise, counterfeit-change, check-in and ATM items are national Argentina advice that applies in BA. The city radio-taxi list (data.buenosaires.gob.ar, linked by FCDO) could not be fetched (connection dropped), so it is listed as a link only, not quoted.

items.name: Street money changers with old or fake notes
items.what_happens: Street money changers in Cusco tourist areas have passed off intis (a former currency, no longer in circulation), and counterfeit soles and US dollars circulate widely; street changers may also work with pickpockets.
items.avoid: Do not change money on the street; use banks or official exchange offices and check notes you receive.

sources.quote: There have been reports of street money changers in Cusco tourist areas fraudulently using Peruvian intis (former currency now out of circulation).
Avoid moneychangers on the street, as they may carry counterfeit currency or work with pickpockets.

items.name: Unscrupulous tour agents and guides
items.what_happens: Unscrupulous tour agents have targeted young women travelling alone in the Cusco area, and tour guides have been implicated in some sexual assaults.
items.avoid: Book through registered agencies (iPerú can tell you which are reputable), buy your own drinks and keep sight of them, and avoid going alone with a guide you have just met.

sources.quote: Unscrupulous tour agents have targeted young females, travelling alone in the Cusco area.
In some cases, tour guides have been implicated.

items.name: Machu Picchu tickets from informal sellers
items.what_happens: Informal agencies and operators have offered entry tickets to Machu Picchu after they were already sold out; the official tourism site advises verifying agencies and payment account names.
items.avoid: Buy tickets through the Ministry of Culture's official sale channels or in person in Machu Picchu Pueblo, and check that any agency is registered before you pay.

sources.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Dirección Desconcentrada de Cultura Cusco
sources.quote: ofrecen boletos de ingreso, cuando ya se encuentran agotados
Verify the authenticity of the agencies, validate payment account names, and seek official agency information from the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism.

items.name: Fake taxis and express kidnapping
items.what_happens: Criminals posing as taxi drivers rob tourists around airports and bus terminals, and express kidnappings, where victims are forced to withdraw money from ATMs, often involve fake or gang-linked taxi drivers.
items.avoid: Use authorised taxis from inside the airport or bus terminal, a reputable company or a ride-hailing app, or ask your hotel to book; do not hail taxis on the street.

sources.quote: Incidents often involve armed criminals posing as taxi drivers, or taxi drivers working for organised gangs.
Only use authorized cabs located inside airport terminals and bus stations

items.name: Fake police
items.what_happens: Thieves pose as police officers to win victims' trust, and some real officers have demanded money to dismiss minor offences.
items.avoid: Ask to see official ID, note the officer's name, badge number and district, and ask for any fine in writing to pay later.

sources.quote: Thieves also pose as police officers to gain the confidence and cooperation of their potential victims.

items.name: Spill-and-clean distraction thefts
items.what_happens: Street crime is a significant problem in Cusco; a common ruse is spraying a substance on someone and robbing them while "helping" clean it, or asking questions while an accomplice steals.
items.avoid: Refuse help from strangers after a spill, keep moving, and keep bags closed and in front of you.

sources.quote: Street crime, including muggings and thefts, is a significant problem in Lima, Cusco, Arequipa and other major cities.
A common scam involves spraying a substance on victims and then robbing them while pretending to help clean the stain

items.name: Unregulated ayahuasca and San Pedro "cleansing"
items.what_happens: Shamans and others offer "spiritual cleansing" ceremonies to tourists in and around Cusco; the brews are unregulated, people have become seriously ill or died, and sexual assaults have been reported.
items.avoid: Avoid spiritual cleansing and ayahuasca ceremonies.

sources.quote: Shamans and other people offer 'spiritual cleansing' (Ayahuasca or San Pedro) to tourists in the Amazon area, northern Peru and Cusco.
Avoid participating in spiritual cleansing or ayahuasca ceremonies.

cusco-peru.notes: FCDO names Cusco for money changers, tour agents, street crime and ayahuasca; Canada lists Cusco for petty crime. Fake taxis, fake police and spill thefts are national Peru advice. The Cultura Cusco notice (Spanish, published 26 July 2023) is dated; the Ministry's online sale domain has varied (peru.travel in 2023 named machupicchu.gob.pe; recent Ministry notices name tuboleto.cultura.pe), so the item does not name a single domain.

items.name: Scopolamine drugging
items.what_happens: Criminals drug victims with scopolamine or similar drugs in food, drinks, cigarettes, aerosols or even flyers, then rob, assault or express-kidnap them; they often work in teams with women gaining the victim's trust, and Canada names Cartagena.
items.avoid: Never leave food or drinks unattended and do not accept anything from strangers or new acquaintances, including on the street.

sources.quote: Criminals often work in teams, with women easing the victim into a false sense of security.
Criminals can administer drugs through food, drinks, cigarettes, aerosols and even paper flyers.

items.name: Dating-app lures
items.what_happens: Criminals use dating apps and websites to find foreigners travelling alone, then drug and rob them.
items.avoid: Do not go to a stranger's accommodation or invite strangers to yours, and meet only in busy public places.

sources.quote: Criminals use dating applications and websites to identify and lure foreign nationals who are travelling alone and looking to meet local people.
Do not accept invitations from strangers to their accommodation, and do not invite strangers to your accommodation.

items.name: Tourist overcharging
items.what_happens: Scammers in popular tourist areas charge tourists elevated prices for services, food and drink, including on cards.
items.avoid: Ask for a printed price list before ordering, and keep your card in sight.

sources.quote: Card overcharging also happens, especially in popular tourist areas, where scammers target tourists by charging them elevated prices for services, food and drink.

items.name: Fake police checking your money
items.what_happens: People posing as police ask to inspect your documents or money, supposedly to check for counterfeits, and rob you.
items.avoid: Do not hand over money or documents; ask to do it at the nearest police station (CAI), your hotel or another public place.

sources.quote: Criminals posing as police are known to operate in Bogotá and elsewhere. They may ask to inspect money to see if it is counterfeit.
Individuals posing as police officers have approached foreigners to verify their documents or foreign currency with the intent to rob them.

items.name: Express kidnapping in unlicensed taxis
items.what_happens: Express kidnappings, assaults and robberies happen in unlicensed taxis; victims are forced to withdraw cash from ATMs, sometimes held overnight for a second withdrawal.
items.avoid: Book taxis by phone, app or through your hotel or restaurant; do not hail on the street, and use ATMs inside banks or malls in business hours.

sources.quote: There have been reports of express kidnappings, assaults and robberies in unlicensed taxis.
Express kidnappings are frequent and often occur in affluent areas, as well as in tourist areas.

items.name: Unlicensed tour boats
items.what_happens: Unlicensed tour boats that do not meet safety standards have been involved in boating accidents; Canada names Cartagena.
items.avoid: Choose a reputable, licensed boat company and do not board a boat that looks unsafe.

sources.quote: Due to unlicensed tour boats not meeting safety standards, boating accidents have occurred

cartagena-colombia.notes: Canada names Cartagena for scopolamine drugging and unlicensed tour boat accidents (in bulleted lists after the quoted lines); FCDO names the Caribbean coast for street crime. Dating-app, overcharging, fake-police and taxi items are national Colombia advice that applies in Cartagena. No official Cartagena city or police page with scam warnings was fetched.

items.name: Helicopter rescue and cheap-trek scams
items.what_happens: Some trekking guides take inexperienced trekkers up too fast and then call expensive helicopter evacuations they take a cut from; documented scams include unnecessary evacuations, falsified documents and inflated bills.
items.avoid: Book with registered, reputable trekking agencies and helicopter companies, avoid unusually cheap packages, ask for a medical assessment before agreeing to an evacuation, and keep copies of all documents.

sources.quote: some trekking guides taking inexperienced trekkers to high altitudes too quickly, and then calling in expensive helicopter medivacs from which the guides take a cut
There have been documented cases of helicopter rescue and insurance scams in Nepal.

items.name: Pickpockets in Thamel, Sanepa and Kupondol
items.what_happens: Pickpockets and bag-snatchers work airports, buses and the tourist areas of Kathmandu, especially Thamel, Sanepa and Kupondol; crime rises in the September to November festival season.
items.avoid: Keep bags closed and in front of you, carry little cash, and take extra care in the evening and in crowds.

sources.quote: Watch out for pickpockets and bag-snatchers, particularly in airports, on buses and in areas popular with foreign nationals like Thamel, Sanepa and Kupondol in Kathmandu.
Take particular care when walking around Kupandol, Sanepa and Thamel, popular tourist spots in Kathmandu, where pickpocketing is common.

items.name: Drink spiking
items.what_happens: Drinks, snacks, gum or cigarettes offered by strangers may be drugged, putting you at risk of robbery or sexual assault.
items.avoid: Do not leave drinks unattended and do not accept food, drinks or cigarettes from new acquaintances.

sources.quote: Be wary of accepting drinks from strangers and do not leave drinks unattended.
Avoid accepting snacks, beverages, gum or cigarettes from new acquaintances, as these items may contain drugs

items.name: Theft from hotel rooms
items.what_happens: Thefts from hotel rooms occur.
items.avoid: Keep valuables in a hotel safe where possible.

sources.quote: Theft also occurs from hotel rooms.
Keep valuables in a hotel safe if possible.

kathmandu-nepal.notes: THIN: pickpocketing is Kathmandu-specific in both sources. The helicopter-rescue scam happens on treks, not in the city itself, but it is the main official scam warning for Nepal and treks are typically booked in Kathmandu. Spiking and hotel-room theft are national Nepal advice. No Nepal Tourism Board page with scam warnings could be fetched (the TIMS page returned 404).

items.name: Fake motorbike taxi drivers around Pub Street
items.what_happens: Lone women have been sexually assaulted by men claiming to be motorbike taxi drivers in the Pub Street area of Siem Reap.
items.avoid: Be wary of approaches and offers of transport from strangers; arrange rides through your hotel or a ride-hailing app, especially late at night.

sources.quote: lone women being sexually assaulted by men claiming to be motorbike taxi drivers in the Pub Street area of Siem Reap

items.name: Bag snatching from tuk-tuks and motorbikes
items.what_happens: Thieves on motorbikes cut bag straps and snatch bags and phones from tourists on foot, in tuk-tuks and on motorbikes, often causing injury; Canada names Siem Reap.
items.avoid: Carry bags on the side away from the road, do not put bags in a bicycle basket, prefer tuk-tuks with side grills, and keep valuables in the hotel safe.

sources.quote: Thieves will cut bag straps and snatch bags or phones from tourists on foot or in tuk-tuks and on motorbikes, often causing injury.
Theft targeting foreigners is frequent on sidewalks, on motorcycles and tuktuks (rickshaws) in:

items.name: Rigged card games and "meet my family" invitations
items.what_happens: Tourist scams include card games, after which criminals sometimes take travellers to ATMs and force them to withdraw money; FCDO also warns about strangers who befriend you quickly and invite you home to meet their family.
items.avoid: Decline invitations from people who befriend you quickly, and never join card games with strangers.

sources.quote: Scams targeting tourists occur, including card games. The criminals sometimes take travellers to ATMs and force them to withdraw money.
wary if a Cambodian or other foreign national befriends you quickly and invites you to their home or hotel to meet their family

items.name: Fake dollar bills in change
items.what_happens: Travellers have been given fake US dollar bills as change in shops and clubs.
items.avoid: Check that notes you receive are genuine and are not damaged or torn.

sources.quote: Travellers have reported fake dollar bills being given as change in shops and clubs.

items.name: Extra "fees" at land border crossings
items.what_happens: Travellers arriving overland have been asked by border officials for extra charges before being allowed into Cambodia, and individuals offer "help" with documents or transport.
items.avoid: Get an e-visa in advance through the official government service, and be careful about accepting help with paperwork or transport at the border.

sources.quote: Some have reported that border officials demanded they pay extra charges before they can enter Cambodia.
Carefully consider accepting assistance from individuals offering to help with documentation or transportation.

items.name: Theft from luggage on the Phnom Penh bus
items.what_happens: Items have been taken from luggage in bus luggage compartments, especially between Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, and from passengers' bags while they sleep.
items.avoid: Keep valuables and your passport in a bag on your lap, not in the hold, and stay alert on overnight or long journeys.

sources.quote: Items have been removed from luggage stored in the luggage compartments of buses, especially on the journey between Phnom Penh and Siem Reap.
There have been incidents on bus journeys where passengers have had items taken from bags while asleep.

items.name: Drink spiking
items.what_happens: Police have reported drink spiking in some bars visited by foreigners.
items.avoid: Do not leave drinks unattended or accept drinks from strangers.

sources.quote: Police have reported instances of drink spiking in some bars visited by foreign nationals. Do not leave drinks unattended.

siem-reap-cambodia.notes: FCDO names Siem Reap's Pub Street; Canada names Siem Reap for street theft and the Phnom Penh-Siem Reap bus. Card games, fake notes, spiking and border fees are national Cambodia advice; the border item applies to overland arrivals (e.g. from Thailand). Angkor Enterprise is listed only as the official Angkor pass seller; its page does not itself warn about fake tickets, so no ticket scam is claimed. Job scams are centred on Sihanoukville, Poipet and border areas (not listed).

items.name: Unpriced menus and padded bar bills
items.what_happens: Some bars, clubs and restaurants do not show prices, then add surcharges or very high amounts to the final bill; tourists who cannot pay have been taken to a cash machine by security staff.
items.avoid: Ask to see a menu with prices before you order, check the bill before paying, and leave any place whose menu does not show prices. Report incidents to the police rather than arguing on the spot.

sources.quote: Tourists have been taken to cashpoints with demands for the money to pay the bill.
Some scams involve surcharges on final bills for drinks or meals.

items.name: Taxi drivers and street invitations steering you to a bar
items.what_happens: Some taxi drivers take a commission for bringing passengers to certain bars, clubs and restaurants; people approached in the street or in a bar with an invitation to a nearby venue have received very large bills.
items.avoid: Do not ask a taxi driver to recommend a bar or club, and be wary of anyone who invites you on to another venue. Use taxis from a reputable company or a dispatcher.

sources.quote: Some taxi drivers are part of these frauds. They may receive a commission to recommend certain bars, clubs and restaurants to passengers.
Once at the new bar, some travellers fall victim to criminal activity or receive very large bills for drinks and entertainment.

items.name: Taxi overcharging
items.what_happens: Incidents of overcharging by taxi drivers have occurred.
items.avoid: Use only officially marked taxis, book through a dispatcher instead of hailing on the street, and make sure the meter is on.

sources.quote: Incidents of overcharging by taxi drivers have occurred.

items.name: Card skimming and street money exchange
items.what_happens: Fraudsters can copy card details without you noticing, and changing money on the street is a risk.
items.avoid: Use ATMs inside banks where you can, check street ATMs for tampering, keep your card in sight when paying, and never change money on the street.

sources.quote: Fraudsters can steal your card details without you noticing.

items.name: Drink spiking in bars
items.what_happens: There have been reports of drinks being spiked, particularly in Budapest bars, leaving people open to robbery or assault.
items.avoid: Buy your own drinks and keep them in sight.

sources.quote: There have been reports of drinks being spiked, particularly in Budapest’s bars.

budapest-hungary.notes: Both governments describe the bill scam at country level; FCDO names Budapest for pickpocketing and drink spiking. Canada also warns that arguing about overcharging can lead to violence.

items.name: Street touts, spiked drinks and huge card bills
items.what_happens: Street touts approach visitors in English and lead them to bars where drinks are spiked; victims wake with no memory and find large sums charged to their credit card. Japanese police name Kabukicho, Roppongi, Shibuya and Ikebukuro as high-risk areas.
items.avoid: Do not follow street touts into bars, do not accept drinks from strangers or leave yours unattended, and carry only the cards and cash you need for the night.

sources.quote: Victims claim to be approached in English by street touts known as “kyakuhiki”. Do not follow street touts into bars.
There have been incidents of overcharging at bars and clubs.

items.name: Disputes over bar bills
items.what_happens: Arguments with staff and door staff over excessive bills have ended in arrests of foreign visitors, and disputes over overcharging have led to violence.
items.avoid: Agree what you are paying before ordering, and if a bill looks wrong, leave the argument for the police rather than the door staff.

sources.quote: British nationals have been arrested at clubs and bars following disputes with staff and doorpersons over excessive bar bills.
Disputes over overcharging have led to violence.

tokyo-japan.notes: FCDO reports losses from hundreds to tens of thousands of pounds and says most British victims were targeted in Kabukicho, Shinjuku. Canada also lists Shinjuku Golden-gai.
